# Learning paths: per skill an ordered list of modules.  These power (a) the day-by-day roadmap, (b) auto-generated quizzes from the
# "Term: definition" pairs, and (c) the RAG knowledge base (each module is retrievable and citable).
# Format:  M: Module title || Term: definition; Term: definition || practice task
#          project:   mini-project used as the practical verification task
#          check_files / check_keywords: rubric used to verify a submitted GitHub repo or write-up

@Docker
project: Containerize a Spring Boot (or Flask) app plus a MySQL database with Docker Compose and document how to run it
check_files: Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, README.md
check_keywords: dockerfile, compose, image, container, volume, port
M: Containers vs virtual machines || Container: isolated process sharing the host kernel; Virtual machine: full guest OS running on a hypervisor; Image: read-only template used to create containers || Install Docker and run hello-world, nginx and an interactive ubuntu container
M: Images and containers in practice || docker run: creates and starts a container from an image; docker ps: lists running containers; Docker Hub: public registry for sharing images || Pull, tag and remove images; map a container port to your laptop
M: Writing a Dockerfile || FROM: sets the base image; COPY: adds files into the image; CMD: default command run when the container starts; Layer caching: unchanged steps are reused to speed up builds || Write a Dockerfile for a small web app and build it
M: Volumes and networks || Volume: persistent storage that outlives a container; Bridge network: default network letting containers talk by name; Port mapping: exposes a container port on the host || Run a database container with a named volume and connect an app to it
M: Docker Compose || docker-compose.yml: declares multi-container apps in one file; depends_on: controls service start order; Environment variables: configure containers without rebuilding images || Compose an app + database stack and bring it up with one command
M: Best practices || Multi-stage build: uses one stage to build and a slim stage to run; .dockerignore: excludes files from the build context; Non-root user: limits damage if a container is compromised || Shrink your image with a multi-stage build

@REST API
project: Build a small REST service (users or todos) with GET, POST, PUT and DELETE endpoints, JSON validation and proper status codes
check_files: README.md
check_keywords: get, post, put, delete, status, json, endpoint
M: HTTP and REST basics || REST: architectural style using resources addressed by URLs; HTTP method: verb such as GET or POST describing the action; Stateless: each request carries everything the server needs || Use curl or Postman to call a public API and inspect headers and bodies
M: Methods and status codes || GET: reads a resource without changing it; POST: creates a new resource; 201 Created: returned after a resource is successfully created; 404 Not Found: the requested resource does not exist || Map CRUD operations to methods and pick the right status code for each case
M: Designing resources and JSON || Resource naming: use nouns like /users/42 not verbs; JSON: text format used for request and response bodies; Idempotent: repeating the request leaves the same server state (PUT, DELETE) || Design the URL structure and JSON shapes for a small todo API
M: Build your first API || Controller: code that receives requests and returns responses; Request body: data the client sends in POST or PUT; Validation: rejecting bad input with a 400 response || Implement GET and POST endpoints in your framework of choice
M: Errors, pagination and versioning || Pagination: returning large lists in pages using limit and offset; API versioning: keeping old clients working via /v1 style paths; Error payload: consistent JSON body describing what went wrong || Add pagination, validation errors and a /v1 prefix

@Spring Boot
project: Build a Spring Boot REST service with a MySQL or H2 database, layered controller/service/repository code and unit tests
check_files: pom.xml, README.md
check_keywords: controller, service, repository, entity, application.properties, restcontroller
M: Spring Boot foundations || Auto-configuration: Spring Boot sets sensible defaults from the libraries on the classpath; Starter: one dependency that pulls in a whole feature set; Spring Initializr: web tool that generates a project skeleton || Generate a project with Spring Initializr and run a hello endpoint
M: Controllers and request mapping || @RestController: marks a class whose methods return JSON responses; @GetMapping: maps an HTTP GET request to a method; @RequestBody: binds the JSON request body to a Java object || Create GET and POST endpoints for a Student or Product resource
M: Dependency injection and layers || Bean: object managed by the Spring container; @Service: marks business logic classes; Dependency injection: Spring supplies collaborators instead of you calling new || Split your code into controller, service and repository layers
M: Persistence with Spring Data JPA || @Entity: maps a Java class to a database table; JpaRepository: gives CRUD methods without writing SQL; application.properties: holds datasource and server settings || Connect your API to MySQL or H2 and persist real data
M: Validation, exceptions and tests || @Valid: triggers bean validation on incoming data; @ControllerAdvice: centralizes exception handling for all controllers; MockMvc: tests controllers without starting a server || Add validation, a global error handler and two controller tests

@Git
project: Create a repository with a README, at least three feature branches merged through pull requests and a resolved merge conflict
check_files: README.md, .gitignore
check_keywords: branch, merge, pull request, commit, conflict
M: Version control basics || Repository: folder whose history Git tracks; Commit: saved snapshot of your files with a message; Staging area: holding zone for changes chosen for the next commit || Init a repo, make five commits and read git log
M: Branching and merging || Branch: independent line of development; Merge: combines the history of two branches; HEAD: pointer to the commit you currently have checked out || Create a feature branch, commit on it and merge it back
M: Remotes and pull requests || git push: uploads local commits to a remote; Pull request: proposes changes for review before merging; Fork: your own copy of someone else's repository || Push to GitHub and open a pull request on your own repo
M: Fixing mistakes || git revert: creates a new commit that undoes an earlier one; Merge conflict: two branches changed the same lines; git stash: temporarily shelves uncommitted changes || Create and resolve a merge conflict on purpose

@SQL
project: Design a small schema (students, courses, enrollments) and write 15 queries using joins, GROUP BY, subqueries and window functions, documented in a README
check_files: README.md
check_keywords: join, group by, having, subquery, index, primary key
M: Querying with SELECT || SELECT: chooses which columns to return; WHERE: filters rows before grouping; ORDER BY: sorts the result set || Answer ten questions on a sample database with SELECT and WHERE
M: Aggregation and grouping || GROUP BY: collapses rows into groups for aggregates like COUNT and SUM; HAVING: filters groups after aggregation; DISTINCT: removes duplicate rows from the result || Compute totals and averages per category and filter groups with HAVING
M: Joins || INNER JOIN: keeps only rows that match in both tables; LEFT JOIN: keeps all rows from the left table plus matches; Foreign key: column referencing another table's primary key || Join three tables to build a report and explain each join type
M: Subqueries and window functions || Subquery: query nested inside another query; Window function: calculates across related rows without collapsing them; CTE: named temporary result defined with WITH || Rank rows per group with ROW_NUMBER and reuse logic with a CTE
M: Design and performance || Primary key: uniquely identifies each row; Index: structure that speeds up lookups on a column; Normalization: organizing tables to reduce redundancy || Create tables with keys and compare a query plan before and after adding an index

@DSA
project: Solve and document 30 problems across arrays, strings, hash maps, linked lists, trees and dynamic programming with complexity analysis for each
check_files: README.md
check_keywords: complexity, o(n), array, tree, hash, recursion, dynamic programming
M: Complexity and arrays || Big-O: describes how running time grows with input size; Array: contiguous block giving O(1) access by index; Two pointers: technique scanning from both ends or at two speeds || Solve five array and two-pointer problems and state each complexity
M: Hashing and strings || Hash map: key-value store with average O(1) lookup; Sliding window: maintains a moving range to avoid re-scanning; Anagram: words with the same letters in different order || Solve five hash map and sliding window problems
M: Stacks, queues and linked lists || Stack: last-in first-out structure; Queue: first-in first-out structure; Linked list: nodes connected by pointers || Implement a stack, a queue and reverse a linked list
M: Recursion, trees and graphs || Recursion: a function solving a problem by calling itself on smaller inputs; Binary search tree: tree where left values are smaller and right values larger; BFS: explores a graph level by level using a queue || Implement tree traversals and BFS/DFS on a graph
M: Sorting and searching || Binary search: halves a sorted search space each step in O(log n); Merge sort: divide and conquer sort running in O(n log n); Quick sort: partitions around a pivot, O(n log n) on average || Implement binary search, merge sort and quick sort from scratch
M: Dynamic programming || Memoization: caches results of overlapping subproblems; Optimal substructure: best solution is built from best sub-solutions; Tabulation: fills a table bottom-up instead of recursing || Solve climbing stairs, knapsack and longest common subsequence

M: Object-oriented Python || Class: blueprint for objects; __init__: constructor that sets up a new object; Inheritance: a class reusing another class's behaviour || Model a bank account or inventory with classes
M: Files, errors and libraries || try/except: catches and handles runtime errors; with statement: opens a file and guarantees it is closed; pip: installs third-party packages || Read a CSV, handle bad rows and call a public API with requests
M: Testing and packaging || pytest: framework for writing concise tests; Virtual environment: isolated set of installed packages per project; requirements.txt: lists a project's dependencies || Add tests for your utility and freeze its requirements

@Statistics

M: Descriptive statistics || Mean: arithmetic average; Median: middle value, robust to outliers; Standard deviation: typical distance of values from the mean || Summarise a dataset with mean, median and spread
M: Probability and distributions || Probability: number between 0 and 1 measuring how likely an event is; Normal distribution: symmetric bell-shaped distribution; Independence: one event does not change the probability of another || Simulate coin flips and dice to see the law of large numbers
M: Inference || Hypothesis test: procedure deciding if data supports a claim; p-value: probability of data at least this extreme if the null were true; Confidence interval: range likely to contain the true value || Run a t-test and interpret the p-value in plain words
M: Regression || Correlation: strength of a linear relationship; Regression coefficient: change in outcome for a one unit change in a predictor; R-squared: share of variance explained by the model || Fit a regression and check residuals

check_keywords: assert, mock, test, coverage, fixture
M: Unit test basics || Unit test: automated test of one small piece of code; Assertion: statement that must be true for the test to pass; Arrange-Act-Assert: structure of a clear test || Write tests for a calculator or string utility
M: Mocks and coverage || Mock: fake collaborator that records how it was used; Fixture: reusable setup for tests; Code coverage: percentage of code executed by tests || Mock an external call and measure coverage

@System Design

check_keywords: scalability, cache, database, load balancer, trade-off, latency

M: Scaling and trade-offs || Sharding: splitting a database across machines; CAP theorem: a distributed system cannot guarantee consistency, availability and partition tolerance together; Replication: copying data to several nodes for availability || Design a URL shortener end to end

M: Tokens and roles || JWT: signed token carrying claims about the user; Bearer token: token sent in the Authorization header; RBAC: permissions granted through roles || Protect an endpoint so only admins can call it
